title: Reactively Retaining Top Talent Can Create a Real Mess
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post criticizes retention efforts that begin only when a valued employee threatens to leave. The author argues that last-minute pay or perquisite offers teach people that threatening to leave is how to get rewarded and signal to everyone else that they are undervalued. The alternative is an ongoing strategy that starts well before anyone is near the door, combining competitive compensation with sustained investment in people. The author contends that talent stays where leaders track careers and offer growth through coaching, training, job rotation and shadow assignments. The post concludes that retention should happen every day, not only at the moment of risk.
points: Counteroffers made in a scramble reward threats to leave and teach top performers how to extract more in the future.
Colleagues who do not receive special awards may conclude they are undervalued and begin exploring their options.
Competitive pay is necessary but not sufficient, since people mostly want to be invested in.
Ongoing conversations about growth, using training, job rotation, development roles and shadow assignments, drive retention.
People who feel their careers are being tracked will sometimes turn down higher pay elsewhere.
quotes: Leaders then scramble to design retention strategies that focus on compensation or perquisites to persuade those people to stay. In the process, leaders send the wrong message to top talent and often disenfranchise other critical team members who don’t receive similar awards.

Those who do qualify for the special awards learn that the way to get more rewards in the future is to threaten to leave the team. And those who don’t qualify for the awards presume they are undervalued and will sometimes explore their options because of this signaling.

The best retention strategy is ongoing and begins way before anyone threatens to leave. Of course, it begins by keeping pace with competitive compensation and benefits, but it doesn’t rely on those ingredients to keep people satisfied and in their seats.

Investing in the skills and talents of team members is the best retention strategy. The best people want to become even better. They desire the opportunities it takes to grow, develop, and to be promoted.

When a team member feels leaders are tracking their careers and investing in them, they stay put. They will even turn down higher compensation elsewhere to remain at the organization that works so hard to develop them.
